screens.title: IoT Messaging with MQTT
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why MQTT is the messaging backbone for many small IoT systems and how it suits the Raspberry Pi. MQTT is a compact protocol that moves messages between devices through a central broker. That broker accepts published messages and forwards them to subscribers interested in the same topic. On a Raspberry Pi you can run a local broker, publish sensor readings, and subscribe to control messages that toggle GPIO devices like LEDs. During this chapter you will install and test Mosquitto on your Pi, use command‑line publishing and subscribing to verify connectivity, and write Python examples using the paho‑mqtt client to send distance or temperature readings and to react to on/off commands. You will also see how topic naming and simple message payloads keep systems modular. A common misconception is that MQTT is only for cloud systems — in fact it is often run locally on a Pi to coordinate nearby devices. By the end you will be able to set up a broker, publish sensor data, and build a subscriber that controls hardware. Ready to explore practical steps and code examples that you can run on your Pi?

Second, you will install Mosquitto on the Raspberry Pi and use simple command‑line tools to validate that the broker is running. Seeing messages appear in a terminal confirms connectivity. Finally, you will write a subscriber that listens for simple text commands and toggles an LED using gpiozero. Each objective pairs a concept with a practical verification step so you know when you have achieved competency. As you work, notice how topic names keep responsibilities clear and avoid sending too much data at once.

screens.title: MQTT and the Publish‑Subscribe Model
screens.narratorSegment: Start by understanding the publish‑subscribe pattern that MQTT implements. In pub/sub, devices either publish messages to named topics or subscribe to topics to receive messages. A broker sits in the middle and routes messages; publishers and subscribers never need to know about each other. This decoupling makes it simple to add or remove devices without rewriting code on peers. A concrete example: a temperature sensor publishes to the topic home/livingroom/temperature every five seconds. Any number of subscribers — a logger, a dashboard, or a rule engine — can receive those readings simply by subscribing to that topic. A common misconception is that pub/sub requires many network connections between devices; in fact, each device maintains a single TCP connection to the broker and the broker handles distribution. Another misconception is that topics are complex — they are simple strings like home/led or pi/distance. Think of a topic as a channel or mailbox. The important practice is to choose clear topic names that reflect device role and location so messages remain easy to filter. Takeaway: pub/sub reduces coupling, scales to many listeners, and lets you build flexible Pi‑based sensor networks without direct peer wiring. How would you name topics for a set of temperature sensors in different rooms?

keyIdea.title: Publish‑Subscribe Defined
keyIdea.text: Publishers send messages to topics; subscribers receive messages for topics. A broker routes messages so devices remain decoupled.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Publish‑Subscribe Model
Core Concept

Publish‑Subscribe

Devices publish messages to topics. Subscribers listen for topics. The broker routes messages to interested subscribers.

Analogy
Topics are mailboxes; publishers drop mail, subscribers open the mailbox when they care.
Concrete example
A distance sensor publishes readings to pi/distance every two seconds. A logger subscribes to pi/distance to store readings.
Common misconception
Some expect many peer connections; instead, clients keep one connection to the broker and the broker handles fan‑out.
Key Takeaway

Use clear topic names and a single broker connection to keep devices decoupled and scalable.

Topic Examples
Sensor topic
home/livingroom/temperature
Actuator topic
pi/led
Check your understanding
  • Define broker, publisher, and subscriber in one sentence each.
  • Give a topic name for a door sensor in the hallway.
  • Explain why the broker simplifies adding new listeners.

screens.title: Key MQTT Components
screens.narratorSegment: To work with MQTT you need to know five core terms. The broker is the server that accepts client connections and forwards messages between them. The client is any device that connects to the broker — your Raspberry Pi, a phone, or another microcontroller. A topic is the string name used to classify messages, such as home/livingroom/temperature. Publish means sending a message to a topic. Subscribe means telling the broker you want messages for a topic. Finally, QoS stands for Quality of Service and controls delivery reliability. The source material mentions QoS without detailed levels; treat it as a control that trades simplicity for stronger guarantees when you need them. A concrete example combines these pieces: a Pi runs a client that publishes to pi/distance, another client subscribes to pi/distance and logs values, and the broker ties them together. A common mistake is confusing topics with clients — topics are not devices, they are labels for messages. Practice by naming topics for your project and explaining which clients will publish and which will subscribe. That exercise clarifies responsibilities and prevents sending control commands to the wrong topic. What topic structure will you use for sensors and actuators in a single room?

keyIdea.text: Broker routes messages; clients connect; topics label messages; publish and subscribe are actions; QoS adjusts reliability.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key MQTT Components

Core Terms

Broker
Server that receives and forwards messages between clients.
Client
Any device that connects to the broker to publish or subscribe.
Topic
A string label such as home/livingroom/temperature that classifies messages.
Publish / Subscribe
Publish sends a message to a topic. Subscribe requests messages for a topic from the broker.
QoS
Quality of Service controls message delivery reliability as required by your application.
Practical card
Decide topic names for sensors and actuators in your Pi network and document which clients publish or subscribe to each topic.
Misconception
Topics are not devices. Keep names descriptive and hierarchical to avoid accidental overlap of responsibilities.

screens.title: Install and Start Mosquitto
screens.narratorSegment: Installing Mosquitto on a Raspberry Pi is a short sequence of steps that results in a running broker you can test from the command line. First, use the package manager to install the mosquitto package and the mosquitto‑clients package. Then enable the service so it starts at boot, and start it immediately. After the service is running, test the broker with two terminals: one subscribing to a topic and one publishing a message to that topic. Running the subscribe command in one terminal and publishing in the other demonstrates the broker is accepting and forwarding messages. A concrete example is included in the lesson visuals using the exact commands you will run. A common mistake is forgetting to enable or start the service, which leaves clients unable to connect. Another trap is running subscribe and publish on separate machines without verifying the broker address; for local testing use localhost. Takeaway: finish the install and confirm message flow from mosquitto_pub to mosquitto_sub before moving to Python code. This ensures the messaging layer is functional. Install and Start Mosquitto means install mosquitto and mosquitto-clients, enable and start the service, then verify using mosquitto_sub and mosquitto_pub.. In practical terms, commands to install and verify a local broker on the pi. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Mosquitto Installation
Step-by-step
Run these commands on your Raspberry Pi to install and start the Mosquitto broker.
Install and enable
sudo apt install mosquitto mosquitto-clients
sudo systemctl enable mosquitto
sudo systemctl start mosquitto
These commands add the broker and client tools, then ensure the broker runs now and after reboot.
Test with two terminals
Terminal A: mosquitto_sub -t "test/topic" Terminal B: mosquitto_pub -t "test/topic" -m "Hello MQTT"
Seeing the message appear verifies the broker forwards messages correctly.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting to start the mosquitto service.
  • Running publish before the subscriber subscribes locally.
  • Using the wrong broker address when testing from another machine.
Key Takeaway

Install, enable, and start Mosquitto, then verify message flow with mosquitto_sub and mosquitto_pub before writing Python code.

screens.title: Testing with mosquitto_sub and mosquitto_pub
screens.narratorSegment: Command‑line testing is a fast way to validate that the broker and network are working before you write Python. Open two terminal sessions on your Pi. In one session, run a subscribe command for a simple topic name, for example test/topic. In the other, publish a short message to that same topic. When the subscriber displays the message immediately, the broker is forwarding messages correctly. This quick test isolates the messaging layer from your application code so you can fix connectivity first. A concrete example is mosquitto_sub -t "test/topic" and mosquitto_pub -t "test/topic" -m "Hello MQTT". If nothing appears, check that Mosquitto is running and that you are using the correct host and port. A frequent error is a mismatched topic string or an accidental trailing slash. Also remember that local testing uses localhost; if you test from another device supply the Pi's IP address. Once you see messages flow on the command line, you have a reliable baseline for running the Python publisher and subscriber examples that follow. screens.title: Install paho‑mqtt and Publisher Example
screens.narratorSegment: Next, install the Python client library paho‑mqtt and use it to publish sensor readings from your Raspberry Pi. Installing the library is a simple pip command. The example publisher connects to the broker on localhost, reads sensor values from a distance sensor, formats the measurement as a string, and publishes to the topic pi/distance at regular intervals. The key elements are creating a client, connecting to the broker with host and port, and calling publish with a topic and a payload. In the provided code the loop publishes a numeric distance value every two seconds and prints a confirmation. A concrete step: run pip install paho‑mqtt, then copy the example script and run it while a subscriber is listening. A common misunderstanding is that publish will queue forever without a connection; the client needs an active connect call to send messages. Another pitfall is blocking long sensor reads inside the publish loop without a sleep interval; use a short sleep to avoid flooding the broker. Takeaway: the paho‑mqtt client is a minimal and direct way to publish sensor data from a Pi, and printing each publish helps you verify behavior during development.

keyIdea.title: Publisher Pattern
keyIdea.text: Create a paho‑mqtt client, connect to the broker, and publish formatted sensor values at a controlled interval.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Python Publisher
Install
pip install paho-mqtt
After installation, use the client to connect and publish. Keep your scripts simple while testing.
Publisher example
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
from time import sleep
from gpiozero import DistanceSensor

client = mqtt.Client()
client.connect("localhost", 1883, 60)

sensor = DistanceSensor(echo=24, trigger=23)

while True:
    distance = sensor.distance * 100
    client.publish("pi/distance", f"{distance:.1f}")
    print(f"Published: {distance:.1f} cm")
    sleep(2)
Developer tips
  • Print published values to confirm messages are sent.
  • Use a sleep interval to avoid flooding the broker.
  • Ensure the broker is running before starting the publisher.
Key Takeaway

Install paho‑mqtt, connect the client to localhost, and publish formatted sensor readings at a controlled cadence.

screens.title: Publisher: Distance Sensor Example Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the publisher example line by line so you understand how data flows from hardware to the broker. First, the code imports the mqtt client, a sleep helper, and the DistanceSensor from gpiozero. The mqtt. Client object is created and connected to the broker at localhost on the default port. The DistanceSensor object encapsulates trigger and echo pins to measure distance. Inside the while loop the code reads sensor. distance, multiplies by 100 to convert to centimeters, and formats the number as one decimal place. The client. publish call sends the string payload to the topic pi/distance. The print statement mirrors what was published so you see progress locally. The sleep call throttles the loop to run every two seconds. A concrete example: if the sensor reads 0.21, the published payload becomes 21.0 and your subscriber will receive that text. A misconception is to expect structured JSON by default; this example sends a simple string for clarity. If you need richer data, you can format JSON before publishing. Takeaway: keep payloads small and consistent so subscribers can parse them predictably. Can you adapt the loop to publish temperature readings every five seconds instead?

screens.title: Subscriber Example: Control an LED
screens.narratorSegment: The subscriber example shows how to turn messages into hardware actions. The script creates an LED object using gpiozero and defines an on_message callback for the MQTT client. When a message arrives, the callback decodes the payload text and checks for simple commands such as ON and OFF. If the command equals ON the LED is turned on; if OFF it is turned off. The client subscribes to the pi/led topic and then enters a loop that waits for messages indefinitely. A concrete example: sending the payload "ON" via mosquitto_pub will cause the LED to illuminate immediately on receipt. One common mistake is not decoding the payload to a string before comparing; the callback receives raw bytes which must be decoded. Another trap is subscribing after connecting without verifying the subscription succeeded; check console output to ensure subscription is active. Takeaway: handle parsing carefully and keep command formats strict and documented so your actuator code responds predictably. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Subscriber & GPIO
Subscriber example
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
from gpiozero import LED

led = LED(17)

def on_message(client, userdata, msg):
    command = msg.payload.decode()
    print(f"Received: {command}")
    if command == "ON":
        led.on()
    elif command == "OFF":
        led.off()

client = mqtt.Client()
client.on_message = on_message
client.connect("localhost", 1883, 60)
client.subscribe("pi/led")
client.loop_forever()
Behavior to expect
Messages with exact payloads "ON" and "OFF" toggle the LED. The print statement helps you debug incoming messages in real time.
Common pitfalls
  • Forgetting to decode the payload before comparing.
  • Using inconsistent command casing; standardize on one format.
Key Takeaway

Map simple, documented text commands to actuator calls and use console prints to confirm messages arrive and actions execute.

screens.title: QoS and Reliability Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter mentions QoS as the control for message delivery reliability. In practice, QoS lets you choose how strictly the broker and client ensure a message arrives. For simple sensor telemetry where occasional packet loss is acceptable, lower assurance keeps costs and complexity down. For commands that must be executed, stronger delivery guarantees are useful. The important conceptual contrast: higher delivery guarantees reduce the chance of a lost message but can add network overhead or duplicate deliveries that your application must handle. A concrete example: a periodic distance reading can be sent with a lightweight setting because a missed sample will be replaced by the next. An ON/OFF command for an actuator may require stronger guarantees or an acknowledgement pattern to ensure the action was applied. A common misconception is to always select the strongest guarantee; that can cause unnecessary retries and latency. Takeaway: choose the right QoS or delivery approach for each message type based on how critical it is and how tolerant you are of duplicates. Document your choices for each topic so subscribers know how to handle duplicates and retransmissions.

screens.title: Broker Role and Multi‑Device Topology
screens.narratorSegment: In a small IoT network the broker becomes the coordination point for multiple clients. You can connect several Raspberry Pis, microcontrollers, and mobile apps to a single Mosquitto broker so each device either publishes or subscribes to the topics it cares about. The broker handles routing and fan‑out so publishers do not need to track listeners. A practical setup might have one Pi publishing environmental data to home/temperature, a second Pi subscribing for local display, and a third client subscribing for cloud relay or logging. The broker knows which clients have active subscriptions and forwards messages only to those clients. A common misunderstanding is to think the broker stores messages forever; unless messages are retained or persistent sessions are configured, the broker simply forwards messages at publish time. For local projects you will typically run a broker on the Pi that serves devices on the same network. Takeaway: design your topics and client responsibilities before wiring devices so the broker routes messages cleanly and you avoid topic collisions or duplication of function. In this lesson you will learn why MQTT is the messaging backbone for many small IoT systems and how it suits the Raspberry Pi. MQTT is a compact protocol that moves messages between devices through a central broker. That broker accepts published messages and forwards them to subscribers interested in the same topic. On a Raspberry Pi you can run a local broker, publish sensor readings, and subscribe to control messages that toggle GPIO devices like LEDs. During this chapter you will install and test Mosquitto on your Pi, use command‑line publishing and subscribing to verify connectivity, and write Python examples using the paho‑mqtt client to send distance or temperature readings and to react to on/off commands. You will also see how topic naming and simple message payloads keep systems modular. A common misconception is that MQTT is only for cloud systems — in fact it is often run locally on a Pi to coordinate nearby devices. By the end you will be able to set up a broker, publish sensor data, and build a subscriber that controls hardware. Ready to explore practical steps and code examples that you can run on your Pi?

Over a few hands‑on steps you will understand the MQTT publish‑subscribe model, install and run a lightweight broker, send sensor readings from Python, and subscribe to topics to control GPIO. First, you will learn the model that separates publishers and subscribers using named topics and a broker that routes traffic. This conceptual separation makes systems modular and lets many devices coordinate without direct peer‑to‑peer connections. Second, you will install Mosquitto on the Raspberry Pi and use simple command‑line tools to validate that the broker is running. Seeing messages appear in a terminal confirms connectivity. Third, you will use paho‑mqtt in Python to publish sensor values at regular intervals; this shows how real hardware can report state. Finally, you will write a subscriber that listens for simple text commands and toggles an LED using gpiozero. Each objective pairs a concept with a practical verification step so you know when you have achieved competency. As you work, notice how topic names keep responsibilities clear and avoid sending too much data at once.

Each objective has a clear practical check you can complete on your Pi. For the publish‑subscribe model, draw a simple diagram showing a broker and two clients with a named topic and explain why publishers do not send messages directly to subscribers. For Mosquitto installation, run the apt command, enable and start the service, and then use the client tools to confirm a message crosses the broker. For publishing from Python, install the paho‑mqtt package and run a short loop that publishes sensor values every few seconds, observing the output. For subscribing and controlling GPIO, implement a message handler that decodes text commands and calls the appropriate gpiozero methods to switch an LED on or off. These verifications are lightweight but conclusive: if the broker routes messages and the LED responds, your chain from sensor to actuator is working. As you test, watch for common mistakes like mismatched topic strings or forgetting to start the broker before clients connect.

Start by understanding the publish‑subscribe pattern that MQTT implements. In pub/sub, devices either publish messages to named topics or subscribe to topics to receive messages. A broker sits in the middle and routes messages; publishers and subscribers never need to know about each other. This decoupling makes it simple to add or remove devices without rewriting code on peers. A concrete example: a temperature sensor publishes to the topic home/livingroom/temperature every five seconds. Any number of subscribers — a logger, a dashboard, or a rule engine — can receive those readings simply by subscribing to that topic. A common misconception is that pub/sub requires many network connections between devices; in fact, each device maintains a single TCP connection to the broker and the broker handles distribution. Another misconception is that topics are complex — they are simple strings like home/led or pi/distance. Think of a topic as a channel or mailbox. The important practice is to choose clear topic names that reflect device role and location so messages remain easy to filter. Takeaway: pub/sub reduces coupling, scales to many listeners, and lets you build flexible Pi‑based sensor networks without direct peer wiring. How would you name topics for a set of temperature sensors in different rooms?

To work with MQTT you need to know five core terms. The broker is the server that accepts client connections and forwards messages between them. The client is any device that connects to the broker — your Raspberry Pi, a phone, or another microcontroller. A topic is the string name used to classify messages, such as home/livingroom/temperature. Publish means sending a message to a topic. Subscribe means telling the broker you want messages for a topic. Finally, QoS stands for Quality of Service and controls delivery reliability. The source material mentions QoS without detailed levels; treat it as a control that trades simplicity for stronger guarantees when you need them. A concrete example combines these pieces: a Pi runs a client that publishes to pi/distance, another client subscribes to pi/distance and logs values, and the broker ties them together.
